                                          PROJECT NO. 58000

 RULEMAKING TO UPDATE                                  §    PUBLIC UTILITY COMMISSION
 WHOLESALE AND IOU RETAIL                              §
 TRANSMISSION COST RECOVERY IN                         §                  OF TEXAS
 THE ERCOT REGION                                      §


 CONSTELLATION ENERGY GENERATION, LLC’S COMMENTS ON PROPOSAL
 FOR PUBLICATION OF AMENDMENTS TO § 25.192 and § 25.193 and NEW § 25.252

        Constellation Energy Generation, LLC, including its wholly-owned subsidiaries under

Calpine LLC (together, “Constellation”) files these comments on the Public Utility Commission

of Texas (“Commission”) Proposal for Publication of the proposed amendments to 16 Texas

Administrative Code (“TAC”) § 25.192 relating to Transmission Rates for Export from ERCOT

and § 25.193 relating to Distribution Service Provider Transmission Cost Recovery Factors

(“TCRF”) and new § 25.252 relating to Large Load Customer Tariffs (“Proposal”). Constellation’s

business in Texas includes development and ownership of generation and wholesale and retail

market participation in ERCOT. In addition to providing power from natural gas, nuclear and

renewable resources to the ERCOT grid, Constellation has engaged in commercial arrangements

with collocated large load customers to provide power via behind-the-meter configurations.1

Constellation’s interest in this rulemaking is in preserving the viability of opportunities in Texas

to serve data centers and other large loads in addition to traditional customers.




        1
          Among these are behind the meter arrangement between Freestone Energy Center and C1 Freestone 1, LLC,
a data center developer, which the Commission recently approved in Docket No. 58872, Application of Freestone
Power Generation, LLC and C1 Freestone 1 LLC for Approval of a Net Metering Arrangement.
                        I.       INTRODUCTION AND GENERAL COMMENTS

        Constellation appreciates the significant strides that the Commission has made in

implementing Senate Bill 6 (“SB 6”)2 to address various issues related to large load development

and interconnection, including to preserve the reliability of the ERCOT grid for customers of all

classes. The undertaking has been substantial, requiring the opening of various rulemaking

proceedings before the Commission as well as ERCOT revision requests. Notably, certain of those

rulemakings which directly relate to this Proposal have not been finalized and are in various stages

of development.

        Constellation urges the Commission to apply two important standards in this rulemaking.

First, this rule should coordinate with other pending and adopted SB 6 rules, leaving no

inconsistencies or areas requiring further interpretation. Regulatory vagueness and uncertainty

inhibit development of resources serving large loads and among other customer classes alike.

Second, the Commission should also ensure in adopting a rule in this proceeding that it preserves

the fundamental ratemaking principle of allocating costs based on cost-causation principles and

should further ensure that no one customer class is paying for the same costs more than once – this

is particularly important as various rules related to each other are in a state of flux.

         Constellation notes that Project No. 58481, Rulemaking to Implement Large Load

Interconnection Standards (“Interconnection Standards Rule”) is pending the issuance of a

Proposal for Adoption, which, in part, will establish the financial security requirements for a large

load customer to cover: (1) its cost and security obligations for transmission system upgrades that

its load necessitates,3 (2) all direct interconnection costs associated with its load to be paid via a


        2
            Senate Bill 6, 89th Leg. R.S. (2025).
        3
          Project No. 58481, Proposal for Publication of new 16 TAC § 25.194 at § 25.194(f)(10) (“Interconnection
Standards PfP”).

                                                       2
 Contribution in Aid of Construction (“CIAC”),4 (3) the costs of any significant equipment or

services to be procured for its load by the interconnection transmission service provider (“TSP”)

and distribution service provider (“DSP”)5 and (4) a non-refundable interconnection fee

requirement of $50,000 per MW of contracted peak demand.6                            As currently drafted, the

Interconnection Standards Rule PfP allows a large load customer that energizes to be refunded the

amounts of financial security not applied to “outstanding amounts incurred” by the interconnecting

TSP or DSP to fulfill the customer’s request for energization (“TSP/DSP Costs”) according to a

schedule which extends to five years of sustained operation at the customer’s contracted peak

demand.7 For a large load customer that withdraws any portion of its requested peak demand, or

fails to utilize its requested capacity, a large load customer may only be refunded 20% of its

financial security that remains after satisfying TSP/DSP Costs, with the remaining 80% used by

the TSP as an offset to rate base, though CIAC is non-refundable.8

         The Commission must use caution to ensure that the present rulemaking is consistent with

the obligations and refundability concepts set forth in the pending Interconnection Standards Rule

as well as with the plain language of SB 6, under which the Proposal is being implemented. For

example, if large load customers are required to post non-refundable financial security to cover

direct interconnection costs through CIAC under the Interconnection Standards Rule, and the

Commission intends this Proposal to exclude direct interconnection cost recovery through TSP



         4
             Interconnection Standards PfP at 16 TAC § 25.194(f)(9).
         5
             Id. at proposed 16 TAC § 25.194(f)(8).
         6
           Id. at proposed 16 TAC § 25.194(f)(7). Constellation notes that “outstanding costs” are not clearly defined
in the proposed Interconnection Standards Rule and suggests that both that rule and this Proposal would generally
benefit from the Commission providing more clarity on what specific amounts are refundable under the former and
what may or may not be included in TCOS in the latter.
         7
             Proposed 16 TAC § 25.194(i).
         8
             Proposed 16 TAC § 25.194(g) and (h).

                                                          3
 and DSP rates, then it must follow that those same large load customers are not billed under

minimum demand charges for costs whose recovery has been fully accounted for in the

Interconnection Standards Rule requirements. As a further matter of clarification, if the

Commission intends that the Proposal require direct assignment of system upgrade costs

necessitated by large load interconnection requests because security posted for this purpose under

the Interconnection Standards Rule is refundable at some point following energization (if that is,

indeed, the intent of proposed 16 TAC § 25.194(i)), this Proposal should be clarified to indicate

how this direct assignment will practically function. In any event, it cannot be the result that this

Proposal combined with the Interconnection Standards Rule results in large load customers paying

for the same costs twice.9

        The Commission should also ensure that minimum billing demand charges and other

transmission cost of service rates implemented under this Proposal are not assessed on large load

customers whose presence on the ERCOT transmission system predates SB 6, the Interconnection

Standards Rule, and the Proposal. Such existing loads do not have transmission costs for which

they are responsible under this framework and Proposed Interconnection Standards Rule, and thus

they should not be allocated any new system upgrade costs. This prospective application of the

Proposal is also consistent with SB 6, which indicates that large load interconnection standards

should only apply to customers requesting “a new or expanded” large load interconnection;10 this

Proposal is an extension of such standards.




         9
           Constellation notes that the nonrefundable $50,000 per MW of contract peak demand “interconnection fee”
requirement of the proposed Large Load Interconnection Standards rule is in addition to the security required for
system upgrade and direct interconnection costs and is already required under proposed § 25.194(f)(7)(B) to be used
as an offset to TSP rate base.
        10
             PURA § 37.0561(c).

                                                        4
                   II.    RESPONSES TO COMMISSION’S QUESTIONS

   1. Should the values associated with the large load minimum billing demand provisions
      be different for large load customers with different contracted peak demands or
      different non-coincident (NCP) demands?

       The values associated with the large load minimum billing demand provisions should be

based on each individual large load customer’s contracted peak demand, not an across-the-board

standard demand level. This embodies the long-time Commission policy of allocating costs to

customers based on their contribution to creating those costs. An across-the-board demand level

abandons that concept just for the sake of administrative convenience. Proposed § 25.193(d)

requiring retail electric providers (“REPs”) to assess minimum demand charges on large load

customers applies to entities subject to pending § 25.194 (Interconnection Standards Rule) which

defines “contracted peak demand” as “the total non-coincident peak demand that a large load

customer requests that an interconnecting DSP or interconnecting TSP serve at a site as stated [in

an] interconnection agreement.” Accordingly, the large load minimum billing demand provisions

should be based on the demand that each large load customer is building its project to require,

which relate to the transmission costs for which that customer is responsible for creating. The

contracted peak demand measure ensures each large load customer is paying for its proportionate

share of required system capacity.

   2. Should the large load minimum billing demand be:
         a. fixed for 20 years as proposed;
         b. reduced in phases over a period of 20 years; or
         c. extended to a longer time period?

       The large load minimum billing demand should be periodically reduced in phases as

contemplated by subsection (b) to account for the depreciation of transmission system

infrastructure required to serve the large load customer. Constellation proposes that this periodic

adjustment be implemented every 4 years and tracks the base rate case review outlined in § 25.247.

                                                5
 More frequent adjustments would be administratively burdensome to implement and would not

likely result in meaningful adjustments year-over-year. Further, the rule should clarify that,

notwithstanding the provisions of § 25.193(d)(3), the 20-year period that begins with the

imposition of large load minimum billing demand charges for large load customers is only

effective on a prospective basis, and not applicable to large loads which are interconnected and/or

receiving service as of the effective date of the final rule. Additionally, large loads subject to the

minimum billing demand provisions of the rule should not be required to pay such charges until

the effective date of the applicable utility’s implementing tariff. Finally, as prefaced above, the

Commission should consider the financial security already required to be provided in the

Interconnection Standards Rule, because to the extent nonrefundable, minimum billing demand

charges imposed under this Proposal should not result in double-recovery by interconnecting

utilities for the same system costs or associated risks.

   3. Should the large load minimum billing demand be based on some measure of demand
      lower than contracted peak demand and NCP demand? For example, should the large
      load minimum billing demand:
         a. reflect a “ratcheted” demand, wherein the large load minimum billing demand
             is some percentage of the customer’s contracted peak demand or maximum
             NCP demand in the previous year? If so, should the ratchet percentage decline
             in phases over the years, and how?
         b. be based on a “weighted average” minimum billing demand, wherein the large
             load minimum billing demand is some weighted average of the large load
             customer’s contracted peak demand or highest NCP demand over the previous
             year and the large load customer’s 12CP demand? If so, should the percentage
             weighting towards contracted peak demand or NCP demand decline in phases
             over the years, and how?

       No, in general, the large load minimum billing demand should be based on contracted peak

demand since this demand is what large load customers are building their projects to require and

therefore what transmission facilities the TSPs are constructing. Using this standard creates an

incentive for large load customers to be realistic about their actual requested demand when

submitting interconnection requests to ERCOT. This will alleviate concerns that the Commission
                                                  6
 and ERCOT have previously expressed in the context of SB 6 implementation, including in the

Interconnection Standards Rule, with large load customers submitting speculative and excessive

load requests (and requiring transmission overbuild). In the Interconnection Standards Rule, the

Commission proposes that large load customers pay a non-refundable interconnection fee of

$50,000 per MW of contracted peak demand, in part to “weed out” non-firm large load

interconnection requests.11 As a result, basing large load minimum billing demand on contracted

peak demand disincentivizes requests which will “over-build” the system to serve load that may

or may not be required; it also has the benefit of providing ERCOT and the Commission with more

accurate load forecasting. However, the billing of minimum demand charges should be

commiserate with the amount of contracted peak capacity which is available to serve a large load

customer for each billing cycle; if a large load customer has built its facilities and is ready to

commence taking service at its contracted peak demand but it is not authorized to energize or fully

commence taking service at this level because the contracted peak capacity is not available, the

large load customer should not be expected to pay demand charges for unavailable capacity.

       The Commission should not base large load minimum billing demand on NCP demand

because it could result in large loads essentially reserving capacity for which they are not paying.


   4. Should separate rate treatment be applied to a large computational load, defined as
      an entity that is subject to §25.194 of this title (relating to Large Load Interconnection
      Standards) and in which 50% or greater of the demand at the site consists of power
      electronic based load, specifically computational load, such as data centers and
      cryptocurrency mining facilities? Responses to this question should include
      applicable legal support or limitations regarding separate rate treatment for large
      computational loads.




       11
            Proposed 16 TAC § 25.194(d)(10) and (f)(7).

                                                          7
        No. Neither SB 6, nor the long-standing existing cost-based ratemaking standards of the

Commission, support differential rate treatment between computational and other large loads.

Constellation notes that SB 6 does not create (nor suggest that the Commission should create)

different classes of large loads; rather, Section 2 of SB 6 merely defines a “large load customer”

as an entity requesting an interconnection that exceeds the demand threshold adopted under

Subsection (c) and a successor in interest to such an entity.”12 Subsection (c) describes “customers

requesting a new or expanded interconnection where the total load at a single site would exceed a

demand threshold established by the commission based on the size of loads that significantly

impact transmission needs in the ERCOT power region. The commission shall establish a demand

threshold of 75 megawatts unless the commission determines that a lower threshold is necessary

to accomplish the purposes described by Subsection (b)” which are the Commission’s large load

interconnection standards.13 In the Interconnection Standards Rule, the Commission has proposed

defining a “large load customer” as “an entity requesting a new or expanded interconnection where

the customer's total expected non-coincident peak demand at a single site is equal to or exceeds 75

MW.”14 Accordingly, the Commission has not previously interpreted SB 6 as calling for, or

allowing, differential treatment of large computational loads and other large loads.

        Not only is differential treatment not contemplated in SB 6, but there is no reason to

distinguish between computational and other large loads for purposes of this Proposal. The

Commission has historically created customer classes based on their load profile similarities and

responsibility for cost causation, not the type of business or activity in which customers engage.

The costs to the ERCOT system related to rate treatment of large loads are the same regardless of


       12
            PURA § 37.0561(a).
       13
            PURA § 37.0561(c).
       14
            Proposed 16 TAC § 25.194(c)(9).

                                                 8
 “type” of large load. The differences between computational and other large loads related to

behavior (such as flexibility in price responsiveness and the related ability to curtail when system

conditions are tight based on the load’s business model and resulting demand) are relevant to

ERCOT for system reliability purposes, not ratemaking purposes. These concerns are more

appropriately addressed in the ERCOT Protocols.

   5. Should the definition for transmission interconnection costs be broadened to include
      transmission projects that are recommended at the conclusion of a batch study to
      serve the transmission capacity needs of a particular load?

       The Proposal lacks sufficient clarity in its current form as to which transmission costs

associated with new large loads the Commission seeks to exclude from TCOS, including as relates

to this question. Proposed § 25.192(e)(6) explicitly excludes transmission interconnection costs

associated with interconnection agreements signed after the effective date of this section from

inclusion in a TSP’s transmission cost of service or transmission service rates. “Transmission

interconnection costs”, under proposed § 25.192(b)(13) are “costs associated with the facilities

required to physically interconnect or upgrade the interconnection of transmission-level customer,

or a distinct set of transmission-level customers, to the existing transmission network, including

interconnection lines, substation additions or modifications, and associated equipment necessary

to establish or modify service.”

       If the Commission intends that “transmission interconnection costs” translate to the same

“direct interconnection costs” for which large load customers must post nonrefundable CIAC

under the Interconnection Standards Rule, then Constellation discourages the Commission from

broadening the definition as posed by this question because it is unnecessary to do so – those costs

will be assessed directly to large load customers under the Interconnection Standards Rule

regardless of whether they were identified before or following a batch study. If the Commission

intends that “transmission interconnection costs” to be excluded from TCOS also include the
                                                 9
 upgrade costs for which large load customers must post refundable financial security under the

Interconnection Standards Rule, then Constellation has no opinion on the proposed broadening of

the definition as long as the method for subsequent direct assignment of those costs to contributing

large load customers is clearly defined in the Proposal.

       The Interconnection Standards Rule, in the pending PfP, already requires large load

customers to provide financial security in the form of a direct cash payment for “direct

interconnection costs” in the form of CIAC, where “direct interconnection costs” include all costs

associated with facilities built to interconnect the large load customer to the existing ERCOT

system, including radial lines and substation upgrades necessary to interconnect the new large load

customer.15 The PfP does not limit the CIAC security requirement to costs identified by a TSP

before or following a batch study. Further, interconnecting TSPs and DSPs are prohibited under

the proposed Interconnection Standards Rule from seeking recovery of such large load direct

interconnection costs under rates.16 Thus, direct interconnection costs are to be paid out-of-pocket

by large load customers, and CIAC is only refundable through a credit or surcharge as needed to

true-up actual costs once facilities are completed.17 The proposed Interconnection Standards Rule

also requires large load customers to provide financial security for “system upgrades that are

necessary to reliably serve the large load customer.”18 As stated previously, refundability of this

security is based on the extent to which the large load customer withdraws or fails to utilize any

portion of its requested capacity, and if “fully” refundable upon energization (other than to account




       15
            Proposed 16 TAC § 25.194(f)(9)(A).
       16
            Proposed 16 TAC § 25.194(f)(9)(B).
       17
            Proposed 16 TAC § 25.194(f)(9)(C).
       18
            Proposed 16 TAC § 25.194(f)(10).

                                                 10
 for TSP/DSP Costs), security posted for system upgrades is only refundable subject to a schedule

following initial energization and sustained operation after five years.

       Constellation notes that other rate classes will already benefit under proposed § 25.192(k),

which requires TSPs to apply each large load customer’s non-refundable $50,000 per MW of

contracted peak demand “interconnection fee” and forfeited financial security posted under the

Interconnection Standards Rule as an offset to TSPs’ transmission revenue requirement.

   6. If a large load customer is able to reserve transmission capacity irrespective of
      whether the large load customer has energized or is fully using available capacity,
      how should these loads be reflected in the resource adequacy reports and assessments
      and transmission planning studies?

       Constellation suggests that this issue is outside the scope of the Proposal, as large load

forecasting is within the purview of 16 TAC § 25.370. The Commission will need to consider what

it means for transmission capacity to be “reserved” under proposed § 25.252(d)(1) if it is also

subject to reallocation under proposed § 25.252(d)(2) and pursuant to the Interconnection

Standards Rule.19 Resource adequacy reports evolve based on the load forecast, and if a large load

is not utilizing its capacity as expected, the load forecast should be adjusted accordingly. However,

while important topics for consideration, resource adequacy reporting and transmission planning

studies are not directly relevant to cost allocation or rate design issues as contemplated in this

Proposal.

                    III.     COMMENTS ON PROPOSED RULE LANGUAGE

   In addition to the above recommendations, Constellation recommends the below changes to

the proposed rule language:




       19
            See proposed § 25.194(h).

                                                 11
 §25.193. Distribution Service Provider Transmission Cost Recovery Factor (TCRF).


      (a) Applicability. The provisions of this section apply to all investor-owned distribution

         service providers (DSPs) providing distribution service entirely within the Electric

         Reliability Council of Texas (ERCOT) region to retail electric providers (REPs) and other

         customers of the distribution system as set forth in this section.


(d)      Large load minimum billing demand.

         (1)    A REP serving a large load customer, as determined defined by §25.194 of this title

                (relating to Large Load Interconnection Standards) and which energized and/or

                commenced taking service after the effective date of this section, must be charged

                for that customer based upon a minimum billing demand.

         (2)    The minimum billing demand for a large load customer under paragraph (1) of this

                subsection must be the lesser of the greater of:

                (A)     the large load customer’s contracted peak demand, as defined in §25.194 of

                        this title (relating to Large Load Interconnection Standards); or

                (B)     the highest non-coincident peak demand placed by the large load customer

                        on the system in the past year; or the “contracted peak capacity” available

                        to a large load customer, as such term is defined herein.

                (C)     the large load customer’s 12CP demand consistent with the most recent

                        ERCOT 12CP intervals, as defined in §25.192 of this title (relating to

                        Transmission Service Rates).

         (3)    Following Commission approval of a TSP’s tariff or tariff revisions implementing

                this section, A the billing of a large load customer’s subject to this section as



                                                  12
                 described herein billing under this section must commence at the level of available

                service (“contracted peak capacity”) at the time it is available, irrespective of

                whether the large load customer has energized or is fully using available capacity,

                and for a period of no less than 20 years.

         (4)    TSPs shall apply to the Commission for a periodic adjustment of the minimum

                billing demand for large load customers which are subject to this section every four

                years following the commencement of billing such charges consistent with the

                processes and procedures set forth in subsection 25.247 of this chapter.


         The Commission should implement Constellation’s proposed revisions consistent with its

comments to ensure that existing large load customers whose presence on the system predate the

Proposal are not subject to retroactive rates that impose minimum billing demand charges on such

loads. The revisions are also consistent with Constellation’s recommendation that minimum billing

demand charges for new large load customers are based on contracted peak demand, as this

demand is what such customers are building their projects to require. The revisions implement

Constellation’s recommendation that large load customers subject to these requirements must

begin paying minimum billing demand charges only upon the effectiveness of a TSP’s tariff

approving such charges, as it would be premature to impose these costs prior to such approval.

Constellation’s recommendations further codify a periodic adjustment of minimum billing demand

to account for depreciation and specify that calculation of these charges should account for the

amount of contracted peak capacity that is available to a large load customer during each billing

cycle.




                                                 13
 §25.252. Large Load Customer Tariffs.

(a)   Applicability. The provisions of this section apply to all transmission service providers

      (TSPs) providing transmission service within the Electric Reliability Council of Texas

      (ERCOT) region and investor-owned utility distribution service providers (IOU DSPs)

      providing distribution service within the ERCOT region to retail electric providers (REPs)

      and other customers of the distribution system. The provisions of this section govern

      electric service provided to large load customers that are subject to §25.194 of this title

      (relating to Large Load Interconnection Standards) and which energized and/or

      commenced taking service after the effective date of this section.

(e)   IOU-DSP tariff requirements. The following provisions regarding large load customers

      apply to IOU-DSPs and large load customers. Each IOU DSP must include the following

      terms in its tariff:

      (1)     Commencement of billing. Following Commission approval of a tariff or tariff

              revisions implementing this section, Bbilling must commence beginning the first

              billing cycle after the date that transmission capacity is made available to serve the

              large load customer and based on the amount of contracted peak capacity which is

              then-available to serve to the large load customer.

      (2)     Large load minimum billing demand.

              (i)      A large load customer that does not energize at the time that billing

                       commences must be billed based on the lesser of the large load customer’s

                       contracted peak demand or the contracted peak capacity available to a large

                       load customer, until such time as the large load customer energizes and the

                       customer’s contracted peak capacity is available. After such time, the large



                                                14
                         load customer must be billed based on the large load customer’s peak

                        demand.

                 (ii)   Subject to subsection (e)(2)(i) of this section, for the first 20 years after

                        commencement of billing, the large load customer must complete 240

                        consecutive payments based on the greater of:

                        (A)    the large load customer’s contracted peak demand;

                        (B)    the highest non-coincident peak demand placed by the large load

                               customer on the system in the past year; or

                        (C)    the large load customer’s 12CP demand consistent with the most

                               recent ERCOT 12CP intervals, as defined in §25.192 of this title

                               (relating to Transmission Service Rates).


       Constellation proposes the above changes to conform with recommendations made in the

prior section.


                                      IV.     CONCLUSION
       Constellation appreciates the opportunity to offer these comments in response to the draft

Proposal for Publication in Project No. 58000 and would welcome the opportunity to answer any

follow-up questions that Commission Staff may have about these recommendations.

EXECUTIVE SUMMARY OF CONSTELLATION ENERGY GENERATION, LLC’S
COMMENTS ON PROPOSAL FOR PUBLICATION OF AMENDMENTS TO § 25.192
                  and § 25.193 and NEW § 25.252


 •   The Commission should ensure this rule is consistent with the pending Large Load
     Interconnection Standards Rule (§ 25.194) related to financial security requirements for
     direct interconnection costs, system upgrade costs, and other binding commitments, and
     Senate Bill 6, to ensure that large load customers are not paying for the same costs twice
     and to ensure that minimum billing demand charges and other transmission cost of service
     rates contemplated under this rulemaking are only imposed on new or expanded large load
     interconnection requests.

 •   The values associated with the large load minimum billing demand provisions in this rule
     should be based on each individual large load customer’s contracted peak demand, not an
     across-the-board standard demand level or based on NCP demand. The contracted peak
     demand measure ensures each large load customer is paying for its proportionate share of
     required system capacity.
 •   Large load minimum billing demand should be periodically reduced every four years to
     account for the depreciation of transmission system infrastructure required to serve large
     load customers. This adjustment should track the base rate case process in § 25.247.
 •   The 20-year period that begins with the imposition of large load minimum billing demand
     charges for large load customers should only be effective on a prospective basis, and not
     applicable to large loads which are interconnected and/or receiving service as of the
     effective date of the final rule. Large loads subject to the minimum billing demand
     provisions of the rule should not be required to pay such charges until the effective date of
     the applicable utility’s implementing tariff, and the billing of minimum demand charges
     should be commiserate with the amount of contracted peak capacity which is available to
     serve a large load customer for each billing cycle.
 •   Separate rate treatment should not be applied to computational versus other large loads;
     there is no support for this disparity in Senate Bill 6. Differences between large load
     behaviors are appropriately accounted for in the reliability context rather than rate context
     and should be addressed in the ERCOT Protocols.

 FOR PUBLICATION OF AMENDMENTS TO § 25.192 and § 25.193 and NEW §25.252

        Constellation Energy Generation, LLC, including its wholly-owned subsidiaries under

Calpine LLC (together, "Constellation") files these comments on the Public Utility Commission

of Texas ("Commission") Proposal for Publication of the proposed amendments to 16 Texas

Administrative Code ("TAC") § 25.192 relating to Transmission Rates for Export from ERCOT

and § 25.193 relating to Distribution Service Provider Transmission Cost Recovery Factors

("TCRF") and new § 25.252 relating to Large Load Customer Tariffs ("Proposal"). Constellation's

business in Texas includes development and ownership of generation and wholesale and retail

market participation in ERCOT. In addition to providing power from natural gas, nuclear and

renewable resources to the ERCOT grid, Constellation has engaged in commercial arrangements

with collocated large load customers to provide power via behind-the-meter configurations.1

Constellation' s interest in this rulemaking is in preserving the viability of opportunities in Texas

to serve data centers and other large loads in addition to traditional customers.




         1 Among these are behind the meter arrangementbetween Freestone Energy Center and Cl Freestone 1, LLC,
a data center developer, which the Commission recently approved in Docket No. 58872, Application of Freestone
Power Generation, LLC and Cl Freestone 1 LLC for Approval of a Net Metering Arrangement.
                     I.       INTRODUCTION AND GENERAL COMMENTS

        Constellation appreciates the significant strides that the Commission has made in

implementing Senate Bill 6 ("SB 6")2 to address various issues related to large load development

and interconnection, including to preserve the reliability of the ERCOT grid for customers of all

classes. The undertaking has been substantial, requiring the opening of various rulemaking

proceedings before the Commission as well as ERCOT revision requests. Notably, certain of those

rulemakings which directly relate to this Proposal have not been finalized and are in various stages

of development.

        Constellation urges the Commission to apply two important standards in this rulemaking.

First, this rule should coordinate with other pending and adopted SB 6 rules, leaving no

inconsistencies or areas requiring further interpretation. Regulatory vagueness and uncertainty

inhibit development of resources serving large loads and among other customer classes alike.

                   II.     RESPONSES TO COMMISSION'S QUESTIONS

   1. Should the values associated with the large load minimum billing demand provisions
      be different for large load customers with different contracted peak demands or
      different non-coincident (NCP) demands?

       The values associated with the large load minimum billing demand provisions should be

based on each individual large load customer' s contracted peak demand, not an across-the-board

standard demand level. This embodies the long-time Commission policy of allocating costs to

customers based on their contribution to creating those costs. An across-the-board demand level

abandons that concept just for the sake of administrative convenience. Proposed § 25. 193(d)

requiring retail electric providers ("REPs") to assess minimum demand charges on large load

customers applies to entities subj ect to pending § 25.194 (Interconnection Standards Rule) which

defines "contracted peak demand" as "the total non-coincident peak demand that a large load

customer requests that an interconnecting DSP or interconnecting TSP serve at a site as stated [in

anl interconnection agreement." Accordingly, the large load minimum billing demand provisions

should be based on the demand that each large load customer is building its project to require,

which relate to the transmission costs for which that customer is responsible for creating. The

contracted peak demand measure ensures each large load customer is paying for its proportionate

share of required system capacity.

   2. Should the large load minimum billing demand be:
         a. fixed for 20 years as proposed;
         b. reduced in phases over a period of 20 years; or
         c. extended to a longer time period?

       The large load minimum billing demand should be periodically reduced in phases as

contemplated by subsection (b) to account for the depreciation of transmission system

infrastructure required to serve the large load customer. Constellation proposes that this periodic

adjustment be implemented every 4 years and tracks the base rate case review outlined in § 25.247.

                                                5
 More frequent adjustments would be administratively burdensome to implement and would not

likely result in meaningful adjustments year-over-year. Further, the rule should clarify that,

notwithstanding the provisions of § 25.193(d)(3), the 20-year period that begins with the

imposition of large load minimum billing demand charges for large load customers is only

effective on a prospective basis, and not applicable to large loads which are interconnected and/or

receiving service as of the effective date of the final rule. Additionally, large loads subj ect to the

minimum billing demand provisions of the rule should not be required to pay such charges until

the effective date of the applicable utility' s implementing tariff. Finally, as prefaced above, the

Commission should consider the financial security already required to be provided in the

Interconnection Standards Rule, because to the extent nonrefundable, minimum billing demand

charges imposed under this Proposal should not result in double-recovery by interconnecting

utilities for the same system costs or associated risks.

    3. Should the large load minimum billing demand be based on some measure of demand
       lower than contracted peak demand and NCP demand? For example, should the large
       load minimum billing demand:
           a. reflect a "ratcheted" demand, wherein the large load minimum billing demand
              is some percentage of the customer's contracted peak demand or maximum
              NCP demand in the previous year? If so, should the ratchet percentage decline
              in phases over the years, and how?
           b. be based on a "weighted average" minimum billing demand, wherein the large
              load minimum billing demand is some weighted average of the large load
              customer's contracted peak demand or highest NCP demand over the previous
              year and the large load customer's 12CP demand? If so, should the percentage
              weighting towards contracted peak demand or NCP demand decline in phases
              over the years, and how?

       No, in general, the large load minimum billing demand should be based on contracted peak

demand since this demand is what large load customers are building their projects to require and

therefore what transmission facilities the TSPs are constructing. Using this standard creates an

incentive for large load customers to be realistic about their actual requested demand when

submitting interconnection requests to ERCOT. This will alleviate concerns that the Commission

                                                  6
 and ERCOT have previously expressed in the context of SB 6 implementation, including in the

Interconnection Standards Rule, with large load customers submitting speculative and excessive

load requests (and requiring transmission overbuild). In the Interconnection Standards Rule, the

Commission proposes that large load customers pay a non-refundable interconnection fee of

$50,000 per MW of contracted peak demand, in part to "weed out" non-firm large load

interconnection requests.11 As a result, basing large load minimum billing demand on contracted

peak demand disincentivizes requests which will "over-build" the system to serve load that may

or may not be required; it also has the benefit ofproviding ERCOT and the Commission with more

accurate load forecasting. However, the billing of minimum demand charges should be

commiserate with the amount of contracted peak capacity which is available to serve a large load

customer for each billing cycle; if a large load customer has built its facilities and is ready to

commence taking service at its contracted peak demand but it is not authorized to energize or fully

commence taking service at this level because the contracted peak capacio, is not available, the

large load customer should not be expected to pay demand charges for unavailable capacity.

       The Commission should not base large load minimum billing demand on NCP demand

because it could result in large loads essentially reserving capacity for which they are not paying.

       Standards) and in which 50% or greater of the demand at the site consists of power
       electronic based load, specifically computational load, such as data centers and
       cryptocurrency mining facilities? Responses to this question should include
       applicable legal support or limitations regarding separate rate treatment for large
       computational loads.

        No. Neither SB 6, nor the long-standing existing cost-based ratemaking standards of the

Commission, support differential rate treatment between computational and other large loads.

Constellation notes that SB 6 does not create (nor suggest that the Commission should create)

different classes of large loads; rather, Section 2 of SB 6 merely defines a "large load customer"

as an entity requesting an interconnection that exceeds the demand threshold adopted under

Subsection (c) and a successor in interest to such an entity."12 Subsection (c) describes "customers

requesting a new or expanded interconnection where the total load at a single site would exceed a

demand threshold established by the commission based on the size of loads that significantly

impact transmission needs in the ERCOT power region. The commission shall establish a demand

threshold of 75 megawatts unless the commission determines that a lower threshold is necessary

to accomplish the purposes described by Subsection (b)" which are the Commission' s large load

interconnection standards.13 In the Interconnection Standards Rule, the Commission has proposed

defining a "large load customef' as "an entity requesting a new or expanded interconnection where

the customer's total expected non-coincident peak demand at a single site is equal to or exceeds 75

MW."14 Accordingly, the Commission has not previously interpreted SB 6 as calling for, or

allowing, differential treatment of large computational loads and other large loads.

        Not only is differential treatment not contemplated in SB 6, but there is no reason to

distinguish between computational and other large loads for purposes of this Proposal. The

Commission has historically created customer classes based on their load profile similarities and

responsibility for cost causation, not the type of business or activity in which customers engage.

The costs to the ERCOT system related to rate treatment of large loads are the same regardless of

    5. Should the definition for transmission interconnection costs be broadened to include
       transmission projects that are recommended at the conclusion of a batch study to
       serve the transmission capacity needs of a particular load?

        The Proposal lacks sufficient clarity in its current form as to which transmission costs

associated with new large loads the Commission seeks to exclude from TCOS, including as relates

to this question . Proposed § 25 . 192 ( e )( 6 ) explicitly excludes transmission interconnection costs

associated with interconnection agreements signed after the effective date of this section from

inclusion in a TSP' s transmission cost of service or transmission service rates. "Transmission

interconnection costs", under proposed § 25.192(b)(13) are "costs associated with the facilities

required to physically interconnect or upgrade the interconnection of transmission-level customer,

or a distinct set of transmission-level customers, to the existing transmission network, including

interconnection lines, substation additions or modifications, and associated equipment necessary

to establish or modify service."

        If the Commission intends that "transmission interconnection costs" translate to the same

"direct interconnection costs" for which large load customers must post nonrefundable CIAC

under the Interconnection Standards Rule, then Constellation discourages the Commission from

broadening the definition as posed by this question because it is unnecessary to do so - those costs

will be assessed directly to large load customers under the Interconnection Standards Rule

regardless of whether they were identified before or following a batch study. If the Commission

intends that "transmission interconnection costs" to be excluded from TCOS also include the

                                                   9
 upgrade costs for which large load customers must post refundable financial security under the

Interconnection Standards Rule, then Constellation has no opinion on the proposed broadening of

the definition as long as the methodfor subsequent direct assignment ofthose costs to contributing

large load customers is clearly defined in the Proposal.

       The Interconnection Standards Rule, in the pending PfP, already requires large load

customers to provide financial security in the form of a direct cash payment for "direct

interconnection costs " in the form of CIAC , where " direct interconnection costs " include all costs

associated with facilities built to interconnect the large load customer to the existing ERCOT

system, including radial lines and substation upgrades necessary to interconnect the new large load

customer. 15 The PfP does not limit the CIAC security requirement to costs identified by a TSP

before or following a batch study. Further, interconnecting TSPs and DSPs are prohibited under

the proposed Interconnection Standards Rule from seeking recovery of such large load direct

interconnection costs under rates.16 Thus, direct interconnection costs are to be paid out-of-pocket

by large load customers, and CIAC is only refundable through a credit or surcharge as needed to

true-up actual costs once facilities are completed.17 The proposed Interconnection Standards Rule

also requires large load customers to provide financial security for "system upgrades that are

necessary to reliably serve the large load customer."18 As stated previously, refundability of this

security is based on the extent to which the large load customer withdraws or fails to utilize any

portion of its requested capacity, and if"fully" refundable upon energization (other than to account

   6. If a large load customer is able to reserve transmission capacity irrespective of
       whether the large load customer has energized or is fully using available capacity,
       how should these loads be relle(ted in the resource adequacy reports and assessments
       and transmission planning studies?

       Constellation suggests that this issue is outside the scope of the Proposal, as large load

forecasting is within the purview of 16 TAC § 25.370. The Commission will need to consider what

it means for transmission capacity to be "reserved" under proposed § 25.252(d)(1) if it is also

subj ect to reallocation under proposed § 25.252(d)(2) and pursuant to the Interconnection

Standards Rule.19 Resource adequacy reports evolve based on the load forecast, and if a large load

is not utilizing its capacity as expected, the load forecast should be adjusted accordingly. However,

while important topics for consideration, resource adequacy reporting and transmission planning

studies are not directly relevant to cost allocation or rate design issues as contemplated in this

Proposal.

 •   The Commission should ensure this rule is consistent with the pending Large Load
     Interconnection Standards Rule (§ 25.194) related to financial security requirements for
     direct interconnection costs, system upgrade costs, and other binding commitments, and
     Senate Bill 6, to ensure that large load customers are not paying for the same costs twice
     and to ensure that minimum billing demand charges and other transmission cost of service
     rates contemplated under this rulemaking are only imposed on new or expanded large load
     interconnection requests.

 •   The values associated with the large load minimum billing demand provisions in this rule
     should be based on each individual large load customer' s contracted peak demand, not an
     across-the-board standard demand level or based on NCP demand. The contracted peak
     demand measure ensures each large load customer is paying for its proportionate share of
     required system capacity.

 •   Large load minimum billing demand should be periodically reduced every four years to
     account for the depreciation of transmission system infrastructure required to serve large
     load customers. This adjustment should track the base rate case process in § 25.247.

 •   The 20-year period that begins with the imposition of large load minimum billing demand
     charges for large load customers should only be effective on a prospective basis, and not
     applicable to large loads which are interconnected and/or receiving service as of the
     effective date of the final rule. Large loads subj ect to the minimum billing demand
     provisions of the rule should not be required to pay such charges until the effective date of
     the applicable utility' s implementing tariff, and the billing of minimum demand charges
     should be commiserate with the amount of contracted peak capacity which is available to
     serve a large load customer for each billing cycle.

 •   Separate rate treatment should not be applied to computational versus other large loads;
     there is no support for this disparity in Senate Bill 6. Differences between large load
     behaviors are appropriately accounted for in the reliability context rather than rate context
     and should be addressed in the ERCOT Protocols.
